soil-phys-231.title: Preventing surface sealing and crusting
soil-phys-231.text: A rotary hoe can break a soil crust, but the relief lasts only a short time. Crusting is a symptom of aggregate breakdown, so lasting control means protecting the aggregates. The long-term remedies are less or no tillage, residue or mulch on the surface, cover crops and organic matter to raise aggregate stability. Residue covering even 30% of the surface greatly reduces crusting and gives water pathways in. On very unstable, sodic soils, gypsum promotes aggregation: as it dissolves it adds calcium and raises the salt concentration of soil water. For how crusts form, see {{ref:soil-phys-031}}.

soil-water-156.title: Saturated and unsaturated flow: pushed by gravity, pulled by suction
soil-water-156.text:
Water in soil moves in two quite different ways, and the line between them sits at field capacity ({{ref:soil-water-177}}). Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to field capacity, gravity and differences in water pressure push water away from where it was applied. That is saturated flow. At higher suctions the push gives way to a pull. Water's adhesion to soil solids sets up a suction gradient, which draws water from wetter to drier soil and from macropores to micropores. That is unsaturated flow. The lab manual states the same split in other units: saturated flow at tensions of 0 to -0.3 bar, driven by hydrostatic head, and unsaturated flow at 0.3 to 31 bars, driven by a tension gradient. ({{ref:soil-water-172}} explains these suctions.)

Unsaturated flow is slow, at most about 2.5 cm a day, so roots keep dying back and growing toward moister soil. It slows because the connected wet pathways shrink as soil dries. {{ref:soil-water-193}} therefore depends on water content, and it falls in a very non-linear way as soil dries.

Six factors control infiltration and movement: texture, structure, organic matter, depth to impervious layers such as hardpans or bedrock, water already present, and soil temperature. Warm soils take in water faster, while frozen soils such as permafrost may not absorb it at all, depending on how they froze. The Richards equation gives the rate of change of moisture in unsaturated soil. Lewis Richardson first published it in 1922, and software such as Hydrus solves it numerically.

soil-phys-258.title: Osmosis: why salty soil starves roots of water
soil-phys-258.text:
Salty soil can leave a plant short of water even when the ground is wet. Osmosis explains why. It is the net movement of solvent through a selectively permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration, which is the same as from high to low {{ref:soil-water-172}}. The pressure needed from outside to stop that net flow is the osmotic pressure. It is a colligative property, so it depends on the solute's molar concentration and not on its identity. Osmotic transport is a pressure-driven viscous flow of solvent, not random molecular diffusion.

In a plant cell, osmotic entry of water raises turgor pressure until it equals the osmotic pressure. In a hypertonic solution water leaves and the cell shrinks; in a hypotonic one it swells turgid. Roots take in water and nutrients across cell membranes by osmosis, so excess salt in the soil lowers water uptake and can cause leaf burn.

soil-phys-259.title: The water molecule and what makes it unusual
soil-phys-259.text: Almost everything water does in soil starts with the shape of one molecule. Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom in a bent, polar molecule. It can make up to four hydrogen bonds, which explains its unusual thermodynamic properties. Cohesion and adhesion give high surface tension, 71.99 mN/m at 25 degrees C, and capillary action that lifts water over 100 m in trees. Specific heat capacity is very high at 4184 J/(kg K) at 20 degrees C, with a heat of vaporization of 40.65 kJ/mol. Density peaks at 3.98 degrees C, so between 0 and 3.98 degrees C water shows an unusual negative thermal expansion. Its high dielectric constant makes water an excellent solvent for hydrophilic substances, but not hydrophobic ones. Over long periods it weathers and erodes rock into soil and sediment.

soil-phys-253.title: Adhesion: why water clings to soil
soil-phys-253.text: Water sticks to soil grains, and it takes energy to pull it off. Adhesion is the tendency of dissimilar particles or surfaces to cling to one another, whereas cohesion is that of like particles. It requires energy from chemical or physical linkages, and the physical ones are reversible when enough energy is applied. Proposed mechanisms are mechanical, chemical, dispersive, electrostatic and diffusive. In surface science it almost always means dispersive adhesion, and a low contact angle indicates higher adhesion per unit area. Strength depends on the mechanisms present and the contact area, and liquids that wet a surface make larger contact.

soil-phys-260.title: Surface tension: the skin on a liquid
soil-phys-260.text: A liquid's surface acts like a skin pulled tight. Surface tension is the energy per unit area that comes from a liquid having a surface, or equivalently a force per unit length. Molecules inside a liquid are pulled equally in all directions, but surface molecules are pulled inward, so the surface contracts toward the smallest area. It is a property of the liquid's interface with another medium, not of the liquid alone. It falls as temperature rises and reaches zero at the critical temperature, so a stated value needs its temperature. A curved liquid surface can balance a pressure difference across it, which is the basis of capillary effects.

soil-phys-252.title: Capillary action: water that climbs without a pump
soil-phys-252.text:
Water can climb a narrow tube against gravity with no pump at all. That is capillary action: a liquid flowing in a narrow space without help from external forces such as gravity. It arises from {{ref:soil-phys-260}}, caused by cohesion within the liquid, combined with {{ref:soil-phys-253}} between the liquid and the wall of a small enough tube or pore. In a narrow tube water forms a concave meniscus, the curved surface of the liquid. The contact length scales with the tube radius while the liquid's weight scales with its square, so narrower tubes lift a liquid higher.

Jurin's law gives the rise height, which falls as the tube radius increases. For water at 20 degrees C the rise is 0.7 mm in a tube of 2 cm radius and 70 mm in a tube of 0.2 mm radius. Mercury behaves the other way. Its internal forces exceed those to glass, so it forms a convex meniscus and a reversed capillary effect.

In hydrology the term describes the attraction of water to soil particles. Differences in soil matric potential drive it, moving water from wet to dry soil. Where a high water table meets strong evaporation, capillary rise brings salts to the surface, and breaking the capillary pores is used to stop it.

soil-phys-257.title: Hygroscopy: materials that draw water from the air
soil-phys-257.text: Some materials pull water out of the air and keep it. Hygroscopy is the attracting and holding of water molecules from the surroundings by absorption or adsorption. Many fertilizer chemicals and salts are hygroscopic, and the moisture they hold is usually proportional to relative humidity. Deliquescent materials absorb enough water to dissolve into a solution, at a characteristic deliquescence relative humidity that depends on temperature and crystalline hydrate form. Soil voids stay saturated with water vapor up to the point of maximal hygroscopicity, beyond which a vapor-pressure deficit develops in the pore space.

soil-phys-255.title: The continuity equation: what enters must go somewhere
soil-phys-255.text: Whatever enters a region must either leave it or pile up inside. A continuity equation describes the transport of a quantity, and is a local form of a conservation law. It relates the change of a quantity in a region to the net flux through the boundary, plus any generation (sources) or removal (sinks) inside. In fluid dynamics it says the rate at which mass enters a system equals the rate at which it leaves plus the mass accumulating within.

soil-phys-256.title: The Hagen-Poiseuille equation for flow in a pipe
soil-phys-256.text: How much pressure does it take to push a fluid through a long thin pipe? The Hagen-Poiseuille equation gives the pressure drop for an incompressible Newtonian fluid in laminar flow through a long cylindrical pipe of constant cross section. It assumes a circular pipe much longer than its diameter and no acceleration, and it rests on the mass balance of {{ref:soil-phys-255}}. Above a threshold of velocity and pipe diameter the flow turns turbulent, giving larger pressure drops than the equation predicts. It also fails near the pipe entrance and for low viscosity or wide, short pipes. Poiseuille derived it experimentally in 1838, with Hagen, and Stokes justified it theoretically in 1845.

soil-water-020.title: Horton overland flow: rain faster than the ground can drink
soil-water-020.text: When rain arrives faster than the ground can take it in, the surplus runs off. Horton overland flow is water flowing across the land surface when rainfall exceeds both the soil's capacity to absorb it ({{ref:soil-water-180}}) and its depression storage capacity. It is named for Robert E. Horton, the engineer who first studied it in detail, and is also called Hortonian or unsaturated overland flow. The flow is shallow, sheetlike and fast, so it can erode soil extensively, especially on steep terrain and loose, flat farmland. Impermeable paved surfaces reach it rapidly, and it is common on construction sites and unpaved roads where vegetation has been stripped.

soil-phys-254.title: Capillary pressure: the smaller the pore, the greater the pull
soil-phys-254.text: The smaller the pore, the larger the pressure. Capillary pressure is the pressure difference between two immiscible fluids in a thin tube or pore, arising from forces between the fluids and the solid walls, as in {{ref:soil-phys-252}}. The Young-Laplace equation gives it as pc = 2 γ cos θ / r, with interfacial tension γ, wetting angle θ and effective radius r of the interface. The wetting phase is the fluid that preferentially spreads across the walls. In the porous plate method, a water-saturated sample sits on a saturated plate in a gas chamber; as gas pressure is raised, the water expelled gives the saturation. Beskow defined soil moisture tension as capillary pressure in his work on frost heave.

soil-phys-262.title: Capillary water: held in small pores, only partly usable
soil-phys-262.text: Capillary water is the water held in small soil pores by adhesion and cohesion, the forces behind {{ref:soil-phys-095}}. Only part of it is available to plants. Plant available water is held between field capacity ({{ref:soil-water-177}}) and the permanent wilting point ({{ref:soil-water-178}}), in mesopores.

soil-phys-268.title: The soil water relationship: calibrating a moisture sensor
soil-phys-268.text: A moisture sensor reports a signal, not water itself. A soil water relationship is a graph of a sensor's measured value against soil water content, which acts as a calibration for one soil. Any reading from a {{ref:soil-water-222}} must be interpreted through such a relationship. Once calibrated, sensors quantify plant available water and show whether water flows by gravity, capillarity or osmotic potential. Soil type matters: at a given water potential, water content rises with clay content, because clayey soils have higher porosity and hold more water, as the curves of {{ref:soil-water-153}} show.

soil-phys-261.title: Gravitational water: the part that drains away
soil-phys-261.text: Some water in a wet soil leaves almost at once. Gravitational water is the water that moves through the large soil pores and drains away under gravity. It is the difference between the moisture content at saturation and at field capacity ({{ref:soil-water-177}}). It drains from macropores too fast for plants to use.

soil-phys-263.title: Hygroscopic water: the film that even dry soil keeps
soil-phys-263.text: Even air-dry soil holds water. Hygroscopic water is the thin film of water held on soil particles between the hygroscopic coefficient and the oven-dry state. The coefficient is reached when the last micropore is drained and only films of water surround the particles. Air-dry soil holds water at potentials ({{ref:soil-water-172}}) of -3000 to -10,000 kPa, in equilibrium with pore air at about 98% relative humidity. Soil dried at 105 degrees C to constant weight is oven dry, the reference for expressing water in mineral soils. Unavailable water, held at the wilting point ({{ref:soil-water-178}}), is mostly hygroscopic water held too tightly in micropores for plants.

soil-phys-196.title: Retardation: why contaminants lag behind the water
soil-phys-196.text:
A contaminant does not always travel at the speed of the water that carries it. Retardation by adsorption is the slowing of a contaminant's average movement relative to groundwater because it adsorbs to the soil, measured by a retardation factor. Adsorption holds the contaminant back until the amount set by the adsorption equilibrium has been adsorbed. The factor depends on the chemistry of both the contaminant and the aquifer, and it is analogous to the retardation factor of chromatography. Less soluble contaminants can move hundreds or thousands of times slower than water, so only the more soluble species travel far.

This differs from the spreading described in {{ref:soil-phys-192}} and {{ref:soil-phys-193}}. Unlike diffusion and dispersion, which merely spread a contaminant, retardation changes its global average velocity, so it can be much slower than the water.

Chromatography gives the clearest definition. There the retardation factor R is the fraction of the substance in the mobile phase at equilibrium: the quantity in the mobile phase divided by the total quantity in the system. In planar chromatography, RF is the substance's travel distance over the solvent front's. It always lies between 0 and 1, because nothing outruns the solvent. A spot that travels 2.5 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm gives 0.50.

soil-phys-251.title: The Péclet number: advection against diffusion
soil-phys-251.text: Two kinds of transport compete in any moving fluid, and the Péclet number says which one wins. It is a dimensionless number giving the ratio of advective to diffusive transport rate, the two processes of {{ref:soil-phys-193}} and {{ref:soil-phys-195}}. For mass transfer, Pe = L u / D, with L a characteristic length, u flow velocity and D the diffusion coefficient; it equals the Reynolds number times the Schmidt number. It can also be written as the ratio of diffusion time to advection time. Where Pe is much greater than 1, advection predominates in mass transport because diffusion takes much longer.

soil-phys-250.title: The breakthrough curve: watching a solute emerge from a column
soil-phys-250.text: Feed a solute into one end of a column of porous material and measure what comes out of the other. The result is the breakthrough curve: the course of the solute's concentration at the outlet after a step change in inlet concentration. A fixed bed is purged with a carrier, then the adsorptive is added so that inlet concentration changes in a step, and the outlet concentration is monitored. Chromatography instead uses pulses. Integrating the area above the whole curve gives the material's maximum loading, and the time until the outlet reaches a threshold concentration gives its usable sorption capacity. The curve's shape carries information on mass-transfer properties, which can be found by fitting simplified models to the data. It shows adsorption of the kind described in {{ref:soil-phys-196}} at work. The source page frames this in adsorption engineering; it does not describe the soil-column version.
